records.source: Ἔστιν δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων·
records.gloss: Is now faith of [things] being hoped for [the] assurance, of things [the] proof not being seen;
pieces: Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for, the proof of realities we do not see.

L.1: Now faith is assurance of things being hoped for, proof of things not being seen.

R.1: Faith is what makes us sure that the things we hope for will come. It is proof to us that what we cannot see is real.

decisions.choice: assurance: a firm, settled confidence that gives the things hoped for a present reality for the believer
alternatives: substance, reality (the hoped-for things made real)
decisions.reason: ὑπόστασις literally means what "stands under" something. At 1:3 it is God's very being; at 3:14 it is the confidence believers must hold firm to the end. Here it can be read objectively (faith gives the hoped-for things substance, makes them real now) or subjectively (faith is the firm assurance that they are real). The two are close: faith treats God's promises as solid ground. The parallel word "proof" and the examples that follow, people who acted on what God had said, fit "assurance" well, but the objective sense "reality" remains possible.

decisions.choice: proof: the evidence that convinces, by which unseen things are shown to be real
alternatives: conviction (the inner certainty of the believer)
decisions.reason: ἔλεγχος is the word for a proof or a convincing argument that settles a matter (compare the related verb in John 16:8, "convict"). It is objective in form: faith itself is the proof. Many readers take it of the believer's inner conviction, which comes to much the same thing; the choice here keeps the word's ordinary sense.

decisions.choice: a description of what faith does, linked to the author's words just before
decisions.reason: δὲ ("now") resumes 10:38-39, where the author quoted Habakkuk 2:4, "my righteous one will live by faith", and said "we are of faith". 11:1 describes faith from the angle that matters for this chapter: it holds to what God has promised for the future ("hoped for") and to what cannot be seen (11:3, 7, 27). It is not meant as a complete definition. The Greek puts "faith" in the middle and the two descriptions in balanced lines.

decisions.choice: realities we do not see (B); what we cannot see is real (R)
decisions.reason: πραγμάτων means "matters, things, realities". Balanced says "realities" to bring out that what faith grasps is real though unseen; Readable states it plainly. Both make "we" the ones hoping and seeing, as the general statement implies.

records.heading: What faith is

records.source: ἐν ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐμαρτυρήθησαν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι.
records.gloss: In this for were attested the elders.
pieces: This is how the people of long ago gained God's approval.

L.2: For in this the elders were attested.

R.2: The people who lived long ago had this kind of faith, and God spoke well of them.

decisions.choice: the elders: the people of old, Israel's ancestors in faith, not church officers
decisions.reason: πρεσβύτερος usually means "older" or an elder of a community, but here it means those who lived long ago, the people whose stories follow in 11:4-38.

decisions.choice: were attested: God bore witness to them, in the record of Scripture
alternatives: were well spoken of by people
decisions.reason: The passive ἐμαρτυρήθησαν does not name who gave the witness, but 11:4 says "God bearing witness", so God is the one approving. His witness stands in the Scriptures that tell their stories (11:5, "before he was taken he was attested"). The same verb opens and closes the chapter (11:2, 11:39), framing the whole list.

decisions.choice: This is how ... gained God's approval (B); had this kind of faith, and God spoke well of them (R)
decisions.reason: "In this" refers back to faith (11:1). Balanced and Readable name God as the one who gives the witness (see the meaning decision), and Readable names faith outright.

records.source: πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι θεοῦ, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὸ βλεπόμενον γεγονέναι.
records.gloss: By faith we understand to have been fashioned the ages by a word of God, so that not from [things] appearing the [thing] being seen to have come into being.
pieces: By faith we understand that the ages were set in order by God's word, so that what we see did not come into being from anything visible.

L.3: By faith we understand [that] the ages were fashioned by [the] word of God, so that what is seen has not come into being from things that appear.

R.3: Because we have faith, we understand that God put the universe and all its ages in order by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word. So the things we see were not made out of anything that can be seen.

decisions.choice: the ages: the world and the whole course of its history, created by God
decisions.reason: αἰῶνας is plural, as at 1:2, where God made "the ages" through the Son. It means the created world seen together with its times and eras, everything that exists in space and time. "The universe" gives the sense but loses the idea of time that the word carries.

decisions.choice: by God's word: Genesis 1 ("And God said"); Psalm 33:6, 9
decisions.reason: God created by speaking (Genesis 1:3, 6, 9; Psalm 33:6, 9, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made"). ῥήματι is a spoken word, as at 1:3, where the Son upholds all things "by the word of his power".

decisions.choice: the visible world did not come from anything visible: it came from God's word, which cannot be seen
alternatives: what is seen came from things that do not appear (pointing to the unseen word)
a purpose clause: so that we might know that ...
decisions.reason: The negative μὴ stands before "from things appearing", and most naturally negates the whole clause: the seen world does not have a visible source. That fits the chapter's theme: faith grasps what is not seen (11:1). The construction εἰς τὸ with the infinitive here gives the result of God's creating by his word.

decisions.choice: by faith: faith as the way people receive God's word and act on it
decisions.reason: The dative πίστει ("by faith") begins eighteen sentences in this chapter. It means that it is through faith that people understand, act, endure and receive (11:4, 5, 7, 8 and so on). Here the author starts with "we": the readers' own faith lets them understand creation; then he turns to the people of old.

decisions.choice: By faith (L, B); Because ... had faith (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "By faith" every time the chapter uses this word (11:3-31), so the repetition that drives the chapter is heard as it is in the Greek. Readable says "Because we have faith", "Because Abel had faith" and so on, which is clearer for young readers and still repeats a single pattern through the chapter. This decision covers the whole chapter.

records.source: Πίστει πλείονα θυσίαν Ἅβελ παρὰ Κάϊν προσήνεγκεν τῷ θεῷ, δι’ ἧς ἐμαρτυρήθη εἶναι δίκαιος, μαρτυροῦντος ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ δι’ αὐτῆς ἀποθανὼν ἔτι λαλεῖ.
records.gloss: By faith a greater sacrifice Abel than Cain offered to the God, through which he was attested to be righteous, bearing witness over the gifts of him the God, and through it having died still he speaks.
pieces: By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain's. Through faith he was attested as righteous, since God bore witness about his gifts. And through faith, though he died, he is still speaking.

L.4: By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he was attested to be righteous, God bearing witness over his gifts; and through it, having died, he still speaks.

R.4: Because Abel had faith, he offered God a better sacrifice than his brother Cain did. Because of his faith, God said that Abel was righteous. God showed that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} accepted Abel's gifts. Abel died, but through his faith he still speaks to us.

decisions.choice: Genesis 4:3-10
decisions.reason: Cain brought some of the produce of the ground and Abel the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions; "the Lord looked on Abel and his offering", but not on Cain's (Genesis 4:3-5). Genesis does not say why. The author gives the reason that matters to him: Abel offered by faith.

decisions.choice: greater: of more worth in God's sight
decisions.reason: πλείονα is literally "more". It can mean larger in amount, but here it means better or of greater worth, as the word does at 3:3.

decisions.choice: through which ... through it: through faith
decisions.reason: Both "faith" and "sacrifice" are feminine in Greek, so "which" and "it" could refer to either. The chapter is about faith, and 11:39 sums up all these people as "attested through faith", so faith is the more likely reference. Even so, Abel's faith was shown in his sacrifice, so the two readings are close.

decisions.choice: he still speaks: Genesis 4:10; Hebrews 12:24
decisions.reason: After Abel was killed, God told Cain, "Your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). The author may mean that Abel still speaks through his example of faith, recorded in Scripture; at 12:24 he contrasts Jesus' blood, which "speaks better than Abel's".

decisions.choice: righteous: right with God, as Jesus calls him "righteous Abel" (Matthew 23:35)
decisions.reason: God's acceptance of Abel's gifts was his witness that Abel was righteous. The author links righteousness and faith again at 10:38 and 11:7.

decisions.choice: his brother Cain; to us; God showed that he accepted Abel's gifts
decisions.reason: Readable says who Cain was and who hears Abel speak, and it explains God's "witness over his gifts" as God's acceptance of them (Genesis 4:4).

records.source: Πίστει Ἑνὼχ μετετέθη τοῦ μὴ ἰδεῖν θάνατον, καὶ οὐχ ηὑρίσκετο διότι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ θεός· πρὸ γὰρ τῆς μεταθέσεως μεμαρτύρηται εὐαρεστηκέναι τῷ θεῷ, χωρὶς δὲ πίστεως ἀδύνατον εὐαρεστῆσαι, πιστεῦσαι γὰρ δεῖ τὸν προσερχόμενον τῷ θεῷ ὅτι ἔστιν καὶ τοῖς ἐκζητοῦσιν αὐτὸν μισθαποδότης γίνεται.
records.gloss: By faith Enoch was taken up [so as] not to see death, and not he was found because took up him the God; before for the taking up he has been attested to have pleased the God; \v 6 without but faith impossible to please, to believe for it is necessary the [one] approaching to the God that he is and to the [ones] seeking out him a rewarder he becomes.
pieces: By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death; he could not be found, because God had taken him away. Before he was taken, it was attested of him that he had pleased God.

And no one can please God without faith, since anyone who approaches God has to believe both that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} exists and that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} repays those who search for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.5: By faith Enoch was taken up so as not to see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him up. For before [his] taking up he has been attested to have pleased God.
L.6: And without faith [it is] impossible to please [him], for the one approaching God must believe that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is and [that] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} becomes a rewarder to those who seek {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out.

R.5: Because Enoch had faith, God took him away from the earth, and he never died. People could not find him, because God had taken him. Scripture says that before this happened, Enoch had pleased God.
R.6: No one can please God without faith. Anyone who wants to come near to God must believe that God is real. They must also believe that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gives a reward to those who look hard for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: Genesis 5:21-24 in its Greek wording
decisions.reason: The words "he was not found, because God had taken him" and "he pleased God" follow the Greek translation of Genesis 5:24. The Hebrew says "Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him". The Greek rendering "pleased God" lets the author argue in 11:6 that Enoch must have had faith.

decisions.choice: taken up: moved from this life to God's presence without dying
decisions.reason: μετατίθημι means to move something from one place to another. With "so as not to see death" it means that Enoch did not die but was taken to God, as Elijah was later (2 Kings 2:11).

decisions.choice: he has been attested: Scripture bears witness
decisions.reason: The perfect μεμαρτύρηται points to a witness that still stands: the written record of Genesis 5:22, 24, which says twice that Enoch walked with God (in Greek, "pleased God"). It is the same verb as 11:2.

decisions.choice: a general rule drawn from Enoch: pleasing God requires faith
decisions.reason: Since Scripture says Enoch pleased God, and pleasing God is impossible without faith, Enoch acted by faith. The rule applies to everyone who would approach God, the readers included (10:22). προσέρχομαι is the author's word for drawing near to God in worship and prayer (4:16; 7:25; 10:1, 22).

decisions.choice: that he exists: that God is, and is the true God who acts
alternatives: that he is (in the sense of being who he says he is)
decisions.reason: ἔστιν means that God exists. In the context, believing this goes with trusting that he acts toward people: he rewards those who seek him.

decisions.choice: rewarder: one who pays what is due; God gives the reward he promised
decisions.reason: μισθαποδότης is a rare word for someone who pays wages or gives a reward; the related noun is "reward" in 2:2, 10:35 and 11:26. The verb γίνεται ("becomes") suggests God shows himself to be such a rewarder to those who seek him out.

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: Readable names Scripture as the witness, following the meaning decision on "he has been attested".

decisions.choice: wants to come near to God
decisions.reason: The book's word for drawing near to God is "approach" at Literal and Balanced and "come near" at Readable (4:16; 7:25; 10:22).

records.source: πίστει χρηματισθεὶς Νῶε περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων εὐλαβηθεὶς κατεσκεύασεν κιβωτὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν τοῦ οἴκου αὐτοῦ, δι’ ἧς κατέκρινεν τὸν κόσμον, καὶ τῆς κατὰ πίστιν δικαιοσύνης ἐγένετο κληρονόμος.
records.gloss: By faith having been warned Noah about the [things] not yet being seen, having taken reverent care he constructed an ark for salvation of the household of him, through which he condemned the world, and of the according to faith righteousness he became heir.
pieces: By faith Noah, warned by God about what could not yet be seen, acted with reverence and built an ark for the salvation of his household. Through this he passed sentence on the world, and he came to inherit the righteousness that faith brings.

L.7: By faith Noah, having been warned about things not yet seen, having taken reverent care, constructed an ark for [the] salvation of his household, through which he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness [that is] according to faith.

R.7: Because Noah had faith, he listened when God warned him about things that no one could see yet. He showed respect for God and built a large boat to save his family. By doing this he showed that the world deserved God's judgment. And he received the righteousness that comes by faith.

decisions.choice: Genesis 6:8-22; 7:1
decisions.reason: God told Noah that he would bring a flood, and told him to build an ark for himself and his household; "Noah did all that God commanded him" (Genesis 6:13-22). Genesis calls Noah "a righteous man" (6:9; 7:1), and 2 Peter 2:5 calls him "a herald of righteousness".

decisions.choice: warned by God: given a message from God
decisions.reason: χρηματίζω is used for a divine message or warning (8:5; 12:25; Matthew 2:12). The "things not yet seen" were the flood that had not yet come, which links Noah to faith in 11:1, "proof of things not being seen".

decisions.choice: taking reverent care: acting out of reverence for God
decisions.reason: εὐλαβέομαι means to be careful or reverent; the related noun is "reverence" in 5:7 and 12:28. Noah's care comes from reverence for God's word, not just fear of danger.

decisions.choice: through which: through his faith, shown in building the ark
alternatives: through the salvation of his household
decisions.reason: "Which" is feminine and could refer to faith or to the ark (both feminine in Greek). Faith is the subject of the chapter and governs the next clause too ("the righteousness that is according to faith"), but the faith was visible in the ark itself, so the readings overlap.

decisions.choice: condemned the world: his obedience showed the guilt of the people who ignored God's warning
alternatives: he pronounced judgment on them (as a preacher)
decisions.reason: The "world" here is the human world of Noah's day (Genesis 6:5, 11-13). By believing and acting, Noah exposed their unbelief, as the people of Nineveh will "condemn" Jesus' generation (Matthew 12:41).

decisions.choice: heir of the righteousness that comes by faith
decisions.reason: The author ties righteousness to faith, as in his quotation of Habakkuk 2:4 at 10:38 and as Paul does (Romans 4:13; Philippians 3:9). "Heir" belongs to the chapter's language of inheritance (11:8, 9).

decisions.choice: warned by God
decisions.reason: The meaning decision shows that the warning came from God; Balanced and Readable name him.

decisions.choice: a large boat; showed that the world deserved God's judgment
decisions.reason: Readable explains "ark", an uncommon word for a boat, and spells out the sense of "condemned" given in the meaning decision.

records.source: Πίστει καλούμενος Ἀβραὰμ ὑπήκουσεν ἐξελθεῖν εἰς τόπον ὃν ἤμελλεν λαμβάνειν εἰς κληρονομίαν, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ποῦ ἔρχεται.
records.gloss: By faith being called Abraham obeyed to go out to a place which he was going to receive for an inheritance, and he went out not knowing where he goes.
pieces: By faith Abraham obeyed God's call to leave for a land he would later be given as his own, and he set out without knowing where he was headed.

L.8: By faith Abraham, being called, obeyed to go out to a place which he was going to receive as an inheritance, and he went out not knowing where he was going.

R.8: Because Abraham had faith, he obeyed when God called him. God told him to leave home and go to a land that God would give to him and his family. So Abraham left home, even though he did not know where he was going.

decisions.choice: Genesis 12:1-4
decisions.reason: God said to Abram, "Go from your country and your relatives and your father's house to the land that I will show you", and "Abram went, as the Lord had told him" (Genesis 12:1, 4). Compare Acts 7:2-4.

decisions.choice: being called: he obeyed at once, while the call was still being given
decisions.reason: The present participle καλούμενος puts the call and the obedience together: he obeyed as he was being called. God is the caller, as in Genesis 12:1.

decisions.choice: as an inheritance: a possession God would give to him and his descendants
decisions.reason: κληρονομία is property received as a gift that passes down the family. Abraham himself never owned the land beyond a burial plot (Genesis 23; Acts 7:5); the promise was to his descendants (Genesis 12:7; 15:18), and the author will show that he was looking for more (11:10, 16).

decisions.choice: God's call; given as his own; to him and his family
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the one calling and say plainly what "inheritance" meant here.

records.heading: The faith of Abraham

records.source: πίστει παρῴκησεν εἰς γῆν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ὡς ἀλλοτρίαν, ἐν σκηναῖς κατοικήσας μετὰ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ τῶν συγκληρονόμων τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῆς αὐτῆς·
records.gloss: By faith he lived as an alien in [the] land of the promise as [in] a foreign [one], in tents having dwelt with Isaac and Jacob the fellow heirs of the promise the same;
pieces: By faith he lived as a resident alien in the land of the promise, as if it were someone else's country. He lived in tents, along with Isaac and Jacob, his fellow heirs of that same promise.

L.9: By faith he lived as an alien in the land of the promise, as [in] a foreign [land], dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the fellow heirs of the same promise.

R.9: Because Abraham had faith, he lived in the land God had promised him, but he lived there as an outsider, as if the land belonged to someone else. He lived in tents, and so did his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob. God made the same promise to them too.

decisions.choice: lived as an alien: lived in a place as a foreigner without the rights of a citizen
decisions.reason: παροικέω means to live somewhere as a resident foreigner. Abraham called himself "a foreigner and a resident alien" among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), even in the land God had promised him (Genesis 17:8).
Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents (Genesis 12:8; 18:1; 25:27), and God repeated the promise of the land to each of them (Genesis 13:15; 26:3-4; 28:13; 35:12).

decisions.choice: with Isaac and Jacob: sharing the same tent life and the same promise
alternatives: Abraham lived together with them throughout
decisions.reason: Isaac was Abraham's son and Jacob his grandson. By Genesis' figures Jacob was only a youth when Abraham died (Genesis 21:5; 25:7, 26), so "with" stresses that the three shared the same way of life as fellow heirs, not that they always lived together.

decisions.choice: his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob; God made the same promise to them too
alternatives: the fellow heirs of the same promise
decisions.reason: Readable says who Isaac and Jacob were and explains "fellow heirs of the same promise".

records.source: ἐξεδέχετο γὰρ τὴν τοὺς θεμελίους ἔχουσαν πόλιν, ἧς τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ θεός.
records.gloss: He was awaiting for the the foundations having city, of which designer and maker the God.
pieces: For he was waiting for the city with firm foundations, a city planned and built by God.

L.10: For he was awaiting the city having the foundations, whose designer and maker [is] God.

R.10: Abraham was waiting for a city that would stand firm forever. God is the one who planned that city and built it.

decisions.choice: the city with foundations: the lasting, heavenly city of God
alternatives: an earthly city in the promised land
decisions.reason: Tents have no foundations; the city Abraham waited for does. The author names it later: "a heavenly one" (11:16), "the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem" (12:22), "the city that is to come" (13:14). Compare Psalm 87:1, where God's city has foundations on the holy mountains.

decisions.choice: designer and maker: God planned the city and made it
decisions.reason: τεχνίτης is a craftsman or designer, δημιουργός a builder or maker of something public. Together they say that the city is entirely God's work, not human work.

decisions.choice: a city that would stand firm forever
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the foundations stand for: permanence, in contrast to tents (11:9). The meaning decision supports this.

records.source: πίστει καὶ αὐτῇ Σάρρᾳ δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος ἔλαβεν καὶ παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας, ἐπεὶ πιστὸν ἡγήσατο τὸν ἐπαγγειλάμενον·
records.gloss: By faith also herself Sarah power for begetting of offspring he received even beyond [the] time of age, since faithful he considered the [one] having promised;
pieces: By faith, together with Sarah herself, he received the power to become a father, even though he was past the age for it, since he held that the one who had made the promise was faithful.

L.11: By faith, with Sarah herself also, he received power for [the] begetting of offspring even beyond [the] time of [his] age, since he considered the one who had promised faithful.

R.11: Because Abraham had faith, he was able to become a father with Sarah, even though they were both too old. Abraham trusted God to keep {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} promise.

decisions.choice: Abraham is the one who received power, together with Sarah
alternatives: Sarah is the subject: "By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even past the age, since she considered the one who promised faithful."
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT prints "Sarah herself" in the dative case (αὐτῇ Σάρρᾳ), which most naturally means "with Sarah herself", so the subject of "he received" is Abraham, continuing from 11:8-10. Two things support this: the phrase καταβολὴν σπέρματος literally means "laying down of seed", the father's part in conceiving a child, and the next verse says the children came "from one man" who was "as good as dead" (masculine). On the other side, the oldest manuscripts had no accents or the small mark that shows the dative, so the same letters can be read as the nominative "Sarah herself", making Sarah the subject; she is then named as a woman of faith in her own right, though she laughed at the promise (Genesis 18:12-15). Both readings say that a child was born by faith to an old couple.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text: "with Sarah herself" and nothing more
alternatives: many manuscripts add a word meaning "barren" ("Sarah herself, being barren")
many later manuscripts add "she gave birth" after "the time of age"
decisions.reason: From general knowledge of the manuscripts: a word meaning "barren" appears in some early witnesses, in different positions, and many later manuscripts add "she gave birth", both of which make Sarah the subject. The SBLGNT has neither. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

God promised Abraham, at nearly a hundred, that Sarah, ninety and past childbearing, would bear a son (Genesis 17:17; 18:11). "The Lord did to Sarah as he had promised" (Genesis 21:1). Paul describes Abraham's faith in the same terms: "his own body, already as good as dead" (Romans 4:19-21).

decisions.choice: the one who had promised: God, who is faithful to his word
decisions.reason: The author uses the same words at 10:23: "he who promised is faithful". Faith here is trust that God keeps his promises.

decisions.choice: they were both too old; trusted God to keep his promise
decisions.reason: Readable names God and says that both were too old (Genesis 18:11).

records.source: διὸ καὶ ἀφ’ ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένου, καθὼς τὰ ἄστρα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ τῷ πλήθει καὶ ὡς ἡ ἄμμος ἡ παρὰ τὸ χεῖλος τῆς θαλάσσης ἡ ἀναρίθμητος.
records.gloss: Therefore also from one were born, and that having been made dead, as the stars of the heaven in the multitude and as the sand the by the shore of the sea the countless.
pieces: So it was that from one man, whose body was already as if dead, there came descendants as many as the stars of heaven, as numberless as the sand along the shore of the sea.

L.12: Therefore also from one [man], and that [man] having been made dead, there were born [descendants] as the stars of heaven in multitude and as the countless sand by the shore of the sea.

R.12: That is why so many people came from this one man, even though his body was already worn out and too old to have children. His descendants were as many as the stars in the sky and the grains of sand on the beach. No one could count them.

decisions.reason: God promised Abraham descendants like the stars of heaven (Genesis 15:5; 22:17) and like the sand on the seashore (Genesis 22:17; 32:12). The wording is close to the Greek of Genesis 22:17.

decisions.choice: as good as dead: past the age of fathering children
decisions.reason: νεκρόω means "put to death" or "made dead"; Paul uses it of Abraham's body (Romans 4:19). It is masculine here and refers to Abraham, which supports reading him as the subject of 11:11.

decisions.choice: descendants
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "were born"; the comparison shows that the many descendants of Abraham are meant.

records.source: Κατὰ πίστιν ἀπέθανον οὗτοι πάντες, μὴ λαβόντες τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ἀλλὰ πόρρωθεν αὐτὰς ἰδόντες καὶ ἀσπασάμενοι, καὶ ὁμολογήσαντες ὅτι ξένοι καὶ παρεπίδημοί εἰσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.
records.gloss: According to faith died these all, not having received the promises, but from afar them having seen and having greeted, and having confessed that strangers and sojourners they are on the earth.
pieces: All these died still holding to faith. They did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it, and they openly said that they were foreigners and passing visitors on the earth.

L.13: In faith these all died, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and having greeted [them], and having confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth.

R.13: All these people kept their faith until they died. They did not receive what God had promised them. But they saw it coming in the distance and were glad to welcome it. They said openly that they were only foreigners and visitors on the earth.

decisions.choice: these all: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Jacob, who died still trusting God
alternatives: everyone named so far (but Enoch did not die)
decisions.reason: "These all" are the patriarchs of 11:8-12, who received the promises (Enoch, 11:5, did not die). Κατὰ πίστιν ("according to faith") varies the chapter's "by faith": they died as they had lived, in faith.

decisions.choice: Genesis 23:4; 47:9; compare 1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 39:13
decisions.reason: Abraham told the Hittites, "I am a foreigner and a resident alien among you" (Genesis 23:4), using in Greek the same kind of pair as here, and Jacob spoke of the years of his "sojourning" (Genesis 47:9). The pair also appears in Psalm 39:13 (38:13 Greek).

decisions.choice: having greeted them: welcomed the promises from a distance, like travelers greeting a city they can see but have not yet reached
decisions.reason: ἀσπάζομαι is the ordinary word for greeting someone. Here it is used of the promised things seen far ahead.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text: "having seen them and having greeted them"
alternatives: some later manuscripts add "and having been persuaded of them"
decisions.reason: From general knowledge: a phrase meaning "and were persuaded of them" appears in some later manuscripts and in the text translated by the King James Version, but not in the early manuscripts. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: what was promised; what God had promised them
decisions.reason: "Promises" here means the things promised (the land, the descendants, the blessing). Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: οἱ γὰρ τοιαῦτα λέγοντες ἐμφανίζουσιν ὅτι πατρίδα ἐπιζητοῦσιν.
records.gloss: The [ones] for such things saying make manifest that a homeland they are seeking.
pieces: Those who talk this way are showing that they are in search of a homeland.

L.14: For those saying such things make manifest that they are seeking a homeland.

R.14: When people talk like that, it shows that they are still searching for a land to call home.

decisions.choice: a homeland: one's own country, the land of one's fathers
decisions.reason: πατρίς is the native land, the country one belongs to. People who call themselves foreigners show that they have not yet arrived home.

records.source: καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐκείνης μνημονεύουσιν ἀφ’ ἧς ἐξέβησαν, εἶχον ἂν καιρὸν ἀνακάμψαι·
records.gloss: And if indeed that they were remembering from which they went out, they would have had opportunity to return;
pieces: Had their minds been on the land they came out of, they would have had time enough to turn back.

L.15: And if they had been remembering that [land] from which they went out, they would have had opportunity to return.

R.15: If they had been longing for the land they came from, they could have gone back there.

decisions.choice: remembering: keeping in mind, longing for
decisions.reason: μνημονεύω here means to have one's thoughts on a place, to think of it with longing. The land they left was Ur and Haran (Genesis 11:31; 12:1), and Abraham would not let Isaac go back there (Genesis 24:6-8).

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text: present tense
alternatives: the past tense, in other manuscripts
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT prints the present tense μνημονεύουσιν; from general knowledge, many manuscripts have the past (imperfect) tense. With "would have had" both form a condition that did not happen, and the meaning is the same. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

records.source: νῦν δὲ κρείττονος ὀρέγονται, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ἐπουρανίου.
records.gloss: Now but a better they reach out for, that is a heavenly.
pieces: But as things are, they are reaching out for something better: a homeland in heaven.

L.16: But as it is, they reach out for a better [homeland], that is, a heavenly [one].

R.16: But they were longing for a better home, a home in heaven.

decisions.choice: but as it is: the logical contrast, not "at this time"
decisions.reason: νῦν δὲ sets the real situation against the unreal condition of 11:15, as at 8:6 and 9:26.

decisions.choice: a better, heavenly homeland
decisions.reason: "Better" is one of the author's key words (7:19, 22; 8:6; 9:23; 10:34). "Heavenly" names the true homeland: the heavenly city of 11:10 and 12:22, "the heavenly calling" of 3:1.

decisions.choice: homeland; home
decisions.reason: The adjectives "better" and "heavenly" are feminine in Greek and go with "homeland" (11:14), which English must repeat.

records.source: διὸ οὐκ ἐπαισχύνεται αὐτοὺς ὁ θεὸς θεὸς ἐπικαλεῖσθαι αὐτῶν, ἡτοίμασεν γὰρ αὐτοῖς πόλιν.
records.gloss: Therefore not is ashamed of them the God God to be called of them; he prepared for for them a city.
pieces: So God does not count it a shame to be known as their God, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made a city ready for them.

L.16: Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God; for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has prepared a city for them.

R.16: So God is not ashamed to have people call {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} their God. In fact, God has already made a city ready for them.

decisions.choice: Exodus 3:6, 15
decisions.reason: God called himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6, 15). Jesus used the same words to show that God's people live (Mark 12:26-27). Being called their God means God binds his own name to them.

decisions.choice: for he has prepared a city: the reason God is not ashamed of them
decisions.reason: γὰρ gives the proof: God has already made the city ready (11:10; 12:22; 13:14; compare John 14:2).

decisions.choice: does not count it a shame
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the idea as God not counting it a shame, which keeps the sense of the Greek in a more natural phrase.

records.source: Πίστει προσενήνοχεν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν Ἰσαὰκ πειραζόμενος, καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ προσέφερεν ὁ τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἀναδεξάμενος, πρὸς ὃν ἐλαλήθη ὅτι Ἐν Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα, λογισάμενος ὅτι καὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγείρειν δυνατὸς ὁ θεός· ὅθεν αὐτὸν καὶ ἐν παραβολῇ ἐκομίσατο.
records.gloss: By faith has offered up Abraham the Isaac being tested, and the only son he was offering up the [one] the promises having received, \v 18 to whom it was said that, In Isaac will be called to you offspring, \v 19 having reckoned that even from [the] dead to raise [is] able the God; from where him also in a figure he received back.
pieces: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. The man who had been given the promises was offering up his only son,
the son about whom he had been told, "Your offspring will be named through Isaac."
He counted on God's power to raise people even from the dead, and from the dead, in a figure, he did receive him back.

L.17: By faith Abraham, being tested, has offered up Isaac, and the one who had received the promises was offering up [his] only son,
L.18: [he] to whom it was said, "In Isaac offspring will be called for you,"
L.19: having reckoned that God [is] able to raise even from [the] dead; from where he also received him back, in a figure.

R.17: Because Abraham had faith, he offered his son Isaac as a sacrifice when God tested him. God had made promises to Abraham, and yet Abraham was ready to give up his only son.
R.18: God had told him, "Your family line will come through Isaac."
R.19: Abraham believed that God could even raise the dead. And it was almost as if Isaac came back from the dead when Abraham received him again.

decisions.choice: Genesis 22:1-18
decisions.reason: "God tested Abraham" and told him to offer "your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love" as a burnt offering; Abraham bound him on the altar, and God stopped him and provided a ram (Genesis 22:1-13). God then swore the promise again (Genesis 22:16-17, quoted at 6:13-14).

decisions.choice: has offered up ... was offering up: the offering was complete in Abraham's will, but not carried out
decisions.reason: The perfect προσενήνοχεν presents the sacrifice as done and still standing on record; the imperfect προσέφερεν pictures him in the act of offering. Together they say that in his heart Abraham had already given Isaac, though God stopped his hand.

decisions.choice: only son: his unique son, the son of the promise
alternatives: only (as if he had no other son)
decisions.reason: Abraham also had Ishmael, but Isaac was the only son born of the promise, through whom it would come (Genesis 21:12; 22:2, 16). μονογενής means one of a kind, the only child of its parents (Luke 7:12; John 3:16). The older rendering "only begotten" stresses birth more than the word does.

decisions.choice: Genesis 21:12
decisions.reason: The quotation is from Genesis 21:12, in the same words as the Greek translation, also quoted at Romans 9:7. It shows why the test was so sharp: the son Abraham was told to offer was the one through whom the promise of descendants would be kept.

decisions.choice: will be called: your offspring will be named, counted as yours
decisions.reason: καλέω with "to you" means that Abraham's descendants who carry the promise will be reckoned and named through Isaac's line.

decisions.choice: in a figure: Isaac's return was a kind of resurrection, a picture of rising from the dead
alternatives: figuratively speaking, he received him back (since Isaac was as good as dead)
as a foreshadowing (of the resurrection, perhaps of Christ's)
decisions.reason: παραβολῇ ("a parable, a figure, a comparison") is used at 9:9 for something that points beyond itself. Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a way he did receive Isaac back from death. Whether the author also sees here a picture of the resurrection to come is not stated.

decisions.choice: from where: from the dead
decisions.reason: ὅθεν can mean "from where" or "therefore". Following "from the dead" it most naturally means "from there", that is, from the dead. Elsewhere in Hebrews it means "therefore" (2:17; 3:1), and that reading is also possible.

decisions.choice: Your offspring will be named through Isaac (B); Your family line will come through Isaac (R)
alternatives: In Isaac your seed will be called
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idiom of Genesis 21:12 into plain words.

records.source: Πίστει καὶ περὶ μελλόντων εὐλόγησεν Ἰσαὰκ τὸν Ἰακὼβ καὶ τὸν Ἠσαῦ.
records.gloss: By faith also concerning [things] coming blessed Isaac the Jacob and the Esau.
pieces: By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau with regard to what was still to come.

L.20: By faith also Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come.

R.20: Because Isaac had faith, he blessed his sons Jacob and Esau and spoke about what would happen to them in the future.

decisions.reason: Isaac blessed Jacob, who had come to him in disguise, and then gave Esau a lesser word about his future (Genesis 27). He later blessed Jacob again knowingly, passing on the blessing of Abraham (Genesis 28:3-4).

decisions.choice: blessed: a father's solemn blessing, which spoke of his sons' future
decisions.reason: A father's blessing was taken as a word that would come true (Genesis 27:33, 37). Isaac's faith was that God would bring about what he spoke, after his death.

records.source: πίστει Ἰακὼβ ἀποθνῄσκων ἕκαστον τῶν υἱῶν Ἰωσὴφ εὐλόγησεν, καὶ προσεκύνησεν ἐπὶ τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: By faith Jacob dying each of the sons of Joseph blessed, and worshiped on the top of the staff of him.
pieces: By faith Jacob, at the point of death, blessed each of Joseph's sons, and he bowed low in worship over the tip of his staff.

L.21: By faith Jacob, dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped on the top of his staff.

R.21: Because Jacob had faith, he blessed each of Joseph's two sons when he was about to die. He leaned on the top of his walking stick and worshiped God.

decisions.choice: Genesis 48:1-20
decisions.reason: When Jacob was ill and near death, he blessed Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh, putting the younger ahead of the elder (Genesis 48:14-20).

decisions.choice: Genesis 47:31 in its Greek wording
decisions.reason: The words come from the Greek of Genesis 47:31: "Israel bowed down on the top of his staff". The Hebrew text as now pointed reads "on the head of the bed". The Hebrew words for "bed" and "staff" are written with the same consonants and differ only in their vowels, which were added much later; the Greek translators read "staff".

decisions.choice: two sons; walking stick; worshiped God
decisions.reason: Readable says that Joseph had two sons (Genesis 48:1), uses a plain word for staff, and names God as the one worshiped, which the Greek leaves implied.

records.source: πίστει Ἰωσὴφ τελευτῶν περὶ τῆς ἐξόδου τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ ἐμνημόνευσεν, καὶ περὶ τῶν ὀστέων αὐτοῦ ἐνετείλατο.
records.gloss: By faith Joseph coming to his end concerning the exodus of the sons of Israel made mention, and concerning the bones of him gave instructions.
pieces: By faith Joseph, when his life was coming to an end, spoke of the Israelites' coming exodus and gave orders about his bones.

L.22: By faith Joseph, coming to [his] end, made mention of the exodus of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, and gave instructions concerning his bones.

R.22: Because Joseph had faith, he spoke before he died about the time when God would lead the Israelites out of Egypt. He told them to take his bones with them when they left.

decisions.choice: Genesis 50:24-25; Exodus 13:19; Joshua 24:32
decisions.reason: Joseph said, "God will surely visit you and bring you up out of this land", and made the Israelites swear to carry his bones up from there (Genesis 50:24-25). Moses took the bones with him (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

decisions.choice: the exodus: the departure from Egypt
alternatives: death (the word is also used of a person's departure, Luke 9:31)
decisions.reason: ἔξοδος means a going out or departure. With "the sons of Israel" it means the departure from Egypt, which Joseph foretold about four hundred years before it happened (Genesis 15:13-14).

decisions.choice: when God would lead the Israelites out of Egypt; take his bones with them
alternatives: spoke of the exodus; gave instructions about his bones
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the exodus was and what Joseph's instructions were, from Genesis 50:24-25.

records.source: Πίστει Μωϋσῆς γεννηθεὶς ἐκρύβη τρίμηνον ὑπὸ τῶν πατέρων αὐτοῦ, διότι εἶδον ἀστεῖον τὸ παιδίον καὶ οὐκ ἐφοβήθησαν τὸ διάταγμα τοῦ βασιλέως.
records.gloss: By faith Moses having been born was hidden three months by the parents of him, because they saw fine the child and not they feared the edict of the king.
pieces: By faith, when Moses was born, his parents kept him hidden for three months. They saw what a fine child he was, and they did not fear the king's decree.

L.23: By faith Moses, having been born, was hidden three months by his parents, because they saw the child [was] fine, and they did not fear the edict of the king.

R.23: Because Moses' parents had faith, they hid their baby for three months after he was born. They saw that he was a special child. They were not afraid of the king's command to kill the baby boys.

decisions.reason: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew boy to be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22). Moses' mother "saw that he was fine" and hid him three months (Exodus 2:2). The Greek of Exodus 2:2 uses the same word ἀστεῖον for the child, as does Acts 7:20.

decisions.choice: the faith is the parents': they hid him by faith
decisions.reason: The verb is passive ("Moses was hidden"), but the ones who acted, and so the ones who had faith, were his parents. Exodus 2:2 names only his mother; the Greek translation of that verse says "they hid him", and the author speaks of both parents.

decisions.choice: fine: a beautiful, well-formed child, perhaps marked out by God
decisions.reason: ἀστεῖος means handsome or fine. Stephen says the child was "fine before God" (Acts 7:20). The author does not explain why the child's looks moved his parents to faith; perhaps they saw in him a sign of God's favor.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text: the verse ends here
alternatives: a few manuscripts add a sentence about Moses, when grown, killing the Egyptian because he saw the humiliation of his people
decisions.reason: From general knowledge: one Greek manuscript and some Latin ones add after this verse a sentence drawn from Exodus 2:11-12. It is not in most manuscripts, and the SBLGNT does not include it. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the king's command to kill the baby boys
decisions.reason: Readable says what the edict was (Exodus 1:16, 22).

records.heading: The faith of Moses

records.source: πίστει Μωϋσῆς μέγας γενόμενος ἠρνήσατο λέγεσθαι υἱὸς θυγατρὸς Φαραώ, μᾶλλον ἑλόμενος συγκακουχεῖσθαι τῷ λαῷ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ πρόσκαιρον ἔχειν ἁμαρτίας ἀπόλαυσιν, μείζονα πλοῦτον ἡγησάμενος τῶν Αἰγύπτου θησαυρῶν τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀπέβλεπεν γὰρ εἰς τὴν μισθαποδοσίαν.
records.gloss: By faith Moses great having become refused to be called son of daughter of Pharaoh, \v 25 rather having chosen to be mistreated with the people of the God than temporary to have of sin enjoyment, \v 26 greater wealth having considered than the of Egypt treasures the reproach of the Christ; he was looking away for to the reward.
pieces: By faith Moses, once he was a grown man, would not let himself be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter.
He chose to share the hardships of God's people instead of enjoying sin's pleasures for a short time.
He reckoned that to bear the reproach of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} was worth more than all the riches of Egypt, because he kept his eyes on the reward.

L.24: By faith Moses, having become great, refused to be called [the] son of Pharaoh's daughter,
L.25: having chosen rather to be mistreated together with the people of God than to have [the] fleeting enjoyment of sin,
L.26: having considered the reproach of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he was looking away to the reward.

R.24: Because Moses had faith, when he grew up he refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh's daughter.
R.25: He chose to suffer along with God's people. He did not want to enjoy the pleasures of sin, which last only a short time.
R.26: He thought that sharing the shame that {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} would suffer was worth more than all the treasures of Egypt. He was looking ahead to the reward God would give him.

decisions.choice: Exodus 2:10-15
decisions.reason: Pharaoh's daughter adopted Moses as her son (Exodus 2:10). "When Moses had grown up" (Exodus 2:11, the same Greek phrase as μέγας γενόμενος) he went out to his own people and took their side against an Egyptian. Compare Acts 7:21-24.

decisions.choice: the fleeting enjoyment of sin: the pleasures of Pharaoh's court, which would have meant turning away from God's people
decisions.reason: For Moses, staying at court as an Egyptian prince would have meant denying his people and their God. In Hebrews sin is often this kind of turning away (3:12-13; 10:26). πρόσκαιρος ("for a time") contrasts with the lasting reward.

decisions.choice: the reproach of the Christ: the kind of disgrace God's Anointed bears, which God's people share
alternatives: disgrace suffered for the sake of the Christ
the reproach of God's anointed people (Israel)
Christ's own reproach, shared by Moses because Christ was with God's people (1 Corinthians 10:4)
decisions.reason: The phrase echoes Psalm 89:51-52 (88:51-52 Greek), where God's servants bear the reproach with which enemies taunt "your anointed", and Psalm 69:10, applied to Jesus at Romans 15:3. The author sees the disgrace that God's people suffer for him as one with the disgrace of the Christ, who suffered outside the gate; he calls the readers to "bear his reproach" (13:13; compare 10:33). How exactly Moses shared it the author does not say.

decisions.choice: the reward: what God gives in return
decisions.reason: μισθαποδοσία is the noun related to "rewarder" (11:6); at 10:35 the readers' confidence "has a great reward".

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting. The Greek has the article ("the Christ"), which Literal keeps.

decisions.choice: sharing the shame that the Messiah would suffer; the reward God would give him
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the sense chosen in the meaning decision and names God as the one who gives the reward.

records.source: πίστει κατέλιπεν Αἴγυπτον, μὴ φοβηθεὶς τὸν θυμὸν τοῦ βασιλέως, τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν ἐκαρτέρησεν.
records.gloss: By faith he left Egypt, not having feared the anger of the king; the for invisible [one] as seeing he endured.
pieces: By faith he left Egypt, unafraid of the king's rage, and he held firm as one who saw the unseen God.

L.27: By faith he left Egypt, not having feared the anger of the king; for he endured as seeing the invisible [one].

R.27: Because Moses had faith, he left Egypt. He was not afraid of the king's anger. He kept going because it was as if he could see God, even though no one can see {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: most likely Moses' flight to Midian (Exodus 2:15); possibly the exodus (Exodus 12:31-41)
alternatives: the exodus itself, when Moses led Israel out (Exodus 10:28-29; 12:31-41)
decisions.reason: The order of the chapter (his growing up in 11:24-26, then this, then the Passover in 11:28) points to Moses' first departure, when he fled to Midian (Exodus 2:15). But Exodus 2:14 says that Moses was afraid then, while this verse says he did not fear the king's anger, which fits the exodus better. If it is the flight, the author sees in it not cowardice but faith that looked beyond Pharaoh.

decisions.choice: he endured as seeing the invisible one: he held out as if he saw God, who cannot be seen
decisions.reason: ἀόρατον ("invisible") is used of God at Colossians 1:15 and 1 Timothy 1:17. Moses lived as though God were before his eyes, which is what 11:1 says faith does. καρτερέω means to persevere, hold out.

decisions.choice: the unseen God; God, even though no one can see him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God, whom "the invisible one" means.

records.source: πίστει πεποίηκεν τὸ πάσχα καὶ τὴν πρόσχυσιν τοῦ αἵματος, ἵνα μὴ ὁ ὀλοθρεύων τὰ πρωτότοκα θίγῃ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: By faith he has kept the Passover and the pouring of the blood, so that not the [one] destroying the firstborn would touch them.
pieces: By faith he held the Passover and had the blood spread on the doorframes, so that the one who struck down the firstborn would not touch the Israelites.

L.28: By faith he has kept the Passover and the pouring of the blood, so that the one destroying the firstborn would not touch them.

R.28: Because Moses had faith, he told the people to keep the Passover and to put the blood of the lamb on the doorframes of their houses. Then the destroyer would not harm their firstborn when he killed the firstborn of Egypt.

decisions.choice: Exodus 12:1-30
decisions.reason: Moses told the elders of Israel to kill the Passover lamb and put its blood on the doorframes, "and the Lord will pass over the door and will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike you" (Exodus 12:21-23). That night every firstborn in Egypt died (Exodus 12:29).

decisions.choice: has kept: he instituted the Passover, which Israel still keeps
decisions.reason: The perfect πεποίηκεν suggests an act with lasting effect: the Passover became a permanent feast (Exodus 12:14, 24).

decisions.choice: pouring of the blood: putting the blood on the doorposts
decisions.reason: πρόσχυσις is a pouring or splashing. In Exodus 12:7, 22 the blood was put on the doorposts and lintel with a bunch of hyssop.

decisions.choice: the destroyer and "them": Israel's firstborn
decisions.reason: "The one destroying" is "the destroyer" of Exodus 12:23. "Them" is masculine and refers to the Israelites, whose firstborn were spared.

decisions.choice: had the blood spread on the doorframes; the Israelites; their firstborn
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where the blood was put and whom "them" means (Exodus 12:7, 22-23).

records.source: Πίστει διέβησαν τὴν Ἐρυθρὰν Θάλασσαν ὡς διὰ ξηρᾶς γῆς, ἧς πεῖραν λαβόντες οἱ Αἰγύπτιοι κατεπόθησαν.
records.gloss: By faith they passed through the Red Sea as through dry land, of which a trial having taken the Egyptians were swallowed up.
pieces: By faith Israel went through the Red Sea as if it were dry ground; the Egyptians made the attempt too, and the sea swallowed them.

L.29: By faith they passed through the Red Sea as through dry land; the Egyptians, having made an attempt at it, were swallowed up.

R.29: Because the people of Israel had faith, they walked through the Red Sea on dry ground. When the Egyptians tried to do the same, the water swallowed them up.

decisions.choice: Exodus 14:21-31
decisions.reason: "The Israelites went into the sea on dry ground", and the Egyptians who went in after them were drowned (Exodus 14:22-28; 15:4).

decisions.choice: the Red Sea: the name the Greek Bible gives to the sea of the exodus
decisions.reason: The Hebrew calls it the "Sea of Reeds"; the Greek translation of the Old Testament calls it the Red Sea, as here and at Acts 7:36.

decisions.choice: Israel; the people of Israel
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "they"; Balanced and Readable name the people, since Moses is no longer the subject.

records.source: πίστει τὰ τείχη Ἰεριχὼ ἔπεσαν κυκλωθέντα ἐπὶ ἑπτὰ ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: By faith the walls of Jericho fell having been encircled for seven days.
pieces: By faith the walls of Jericho fell, when Israel had gone around them day after day for seven days.

L.30: By faith the walls of Jericho fell, having been encircled for seven days.

R.30: Because the people of Israel had faith, the walls of the city of Jericho fell down. The people had marched around the walls for seven days.

decisions.choice: Joshua 6:1-20
decisions.reason: At God's command Israel marched around Jericho once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh, and the wall fell down flat (Joshua 6:3-5, 15-20).

decisions.choice: the faith of Joshua and the people
decisions.reason: The walls are the subject, but the faith was that of the people who marched around them as God had told them, without any means of attack.

decisions.choice: Israel; the people of Israel had faith
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name those who marched, and Readable says whose faith it was, following the meaning decision.

records.source: πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη οὐ συναπώλετο τοῖς ἀπειθήσασιν, δεξαμένη τοὺς κατασκόπους μετ’ εἰρήνης.
records.gloss: By faith Rahab the prostitute not did perish with the [ones] having disobeyed, having received the spies with peace.
pieces: By faith Rahab the prostitute escaped the death of those who refused to obey, since she had taken in the spies in peace.

L.31: By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who disobeyed, having received the spies with peace.

R.31: Because Rahab the prostitute had faith, she did not die with the people of her city who refused to obey God. She had welcomed the spies from Israel in peace, as friends.

decisions.reason: Rahab hid the two spies Joshua sent to Jericho, saying "the Lord your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11), and she and her family were spared when the city fell (Joshua 6:22-25). James 2:25 also cites her, and Matthew 1:5 names a Rahab among Jesus' ancestors.

decisions.choice: prostitute
decisions.reason: πόρνη means a prostitute, as does the Hebrew word in Joshua 2:1. Some later Jewish tradition took her to be an innkeeper, but the author's word is plain, and the point is that God received even her by faith.

decisions.choice: those who disobeyed: the people of Jericho, who would not submit to God
decisions.reason: ἀπειθέω means to disobey, and also to refuse belief; Hebrews uses it for the Israelites who did not enter the land (3:18; 4:6). The people of Jericho had heard what God had done (Joshua 2:10-11) and still resisted.

decisions.choice: with peace: as friends, not as enemies
decisions.reason: To receive someone "with peace" means to welcome them peaceably and do them no harm.

decisions.choice: the people of her city; refused to obey God; from Israel; as friends
decisions.reason: Readable says who the disobedient people and the spies were and explains "with peace".

records.source: Καὶ τί ἔτι λέγω;
records.gloss: And what more do I say?
pieces: And what more should I say?

L.32: And what more shall I say?

R.32: What else can I tell you?

decisions.choice: a deliberative question: the author breaks off his list
decisions.reason: λέγω is a subjunctive asking what one should do. The author speaks as "I" here (also 13:19-23) and signals that he will now go faster.

records.heading: More witnesses of faith

records.source: ἐπιλείψει με γὰρ διηγούμενον ὁ χρόνος περὶ Γεδεών, Βαράκ, Σαμψών, Ἰεφθάε, Δαυίδ τε καὶ Σαμουὴλ καὶ τῶν προφητῶν, οἳ διὰ πίστεως κατηγωνίσαντο βασιλείας, εἰργάσαντο δικαιοσύνην, ἐπέτυχον ἐπαγγελιῶν, ἔφραξαν στόματα λεόντων, ἔσβεσαν δύναμιν πυρός, ἔφυγον στόματα μαχαίρης, ἐδυναμώθησαν ἀπὸ ἀσθενείας, ἐγενήθησαν ἰσχυροὶ ἐν πολέμῳ, παρεμβολὰς ἔκλιναν ἀλλοτρίων·
records.gloss: Will fail me for telling the time about Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and also Samuel and the prophets, \v 33 who through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, shut mouths of lions, \v 34 quenched power of fire, escaped mouths of sword, were made strong from weakness, became mighty in war, armies turned back of foreigners;
pieces: Time would run out on me if I told about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, about David and Samuel and the prophets.
Through faith they overcame kingdoms, ruled with justice, won what had been promised, and shut the mouths of lions.
They put out the power of fire, got away from the sword's edge, found strength when they were weak, grew mighty in war, and drove back foreign armies.

L.32: For the time will fail me telling about Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David as well as Samuel and the prophets,
L.33: who through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, shut [the] mouths of lions,
L.34: quenched [the] power of fire, escaped [the] mouths of [the] sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, turned back [the] armies of foreigners.

R.32: There is not enough time for me to tell about Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.
R.33: Because they had faith, they won battles against kingdoms. They ruled fairly. They received what God had promised them. They shut the mouths of lions.
R.34: They put out raging fires. They escaped from being killed with swords. They were weak, but God made them strong. They became powerful in war. They made foreign armies run away.

decisions.choice: the author is a man
decisions.reason: The participle διηγούμενον ("telling") is masculine, agreeing with "me". It is the only place where the letter shows anything about the author's person. It does not say who he was.

decisions.choice: time would fail me: a common way of saying there is too much to tell
decisions.reason: Speakers used this phrase to cut a list short. The author names people and deeds without telling their stories.

decisions.choice: Judges 4-16; 1 Samuel 1 - 1 Kings 2
decisions.reason: Gideon (Judges 6-8), Barak (Judges 4-5), Samson (Judges 13-16), Jephthah (Judges 11-12), David (1 Samuel 16 - 1 Kings 2) and Samuel (1 Samuel 1-25). The names are in pairs, not in the order of Judges: in each pair the better-known figure comes first. "The prophets" covers those whose deeds follow (Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, Jeremiah).

decisions.choice: worked righteousness: ruled with justice, did what was right as leaders
decisions.reason: δικαιοσύνην usually means righteousness; with "worked" and following "conquered kingdoms" it most likely means the just rule of judges and kings (2 Samuel 8:15, David "did justice and righteousness for all his people"; 1 Samuel 12:3-4, Samuel).

decisions.choice: obtained promises: received particular things God had promised, though not the final promise (11:39)
decisions.reason: They saw God keep particular promises: victory, the land (Joshua 21:43-45), the kingdom promised to David (2 Samuel 7). Yet 11:39 says none of them received "the promise", the final inheritance. The plural here and the singular there make the distinction.

Shut the mouths of lions: Daniel (Daniel 6:22; compare Samson, Judges 14:5-6, and David, 1 Samuel 17:34-37). Quenched the power of fire: Daniel's three friends (Daniel 3:19-27). Escaped the edge of the sword: David from Saul (1 Samuel 18-19), Elijah (1 Kings 19:1-3), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24). Made strong out of weakness: Samson (Judges 16:28-30), Hezekiah (Isaiah 38). Turned back foreign armies: Gideon (Judges 7), Jonathan and David (1 Samuel 14; 17). The list may also have in view the Maccabean wars (1 Maccabees).

decisions.choice: the mouths of the sword: the sword's edge
decisions.reason: A Hebrew way of speaking (the "mouth" of the sword, Genesis 34:26), carried into Greek. It also echoes the "mouths of lions" just before.

decisions.choice: ruled with justice; ruled fairly
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense chosen in the meaning decision.

decisions.choice: They were weak, but God made them strong
alternatives: were made strong out of weakness
decisions.reason: The passive "were made strong" implies that God gave the strength; Readable says so.

records.source: ἔλαβον γυναῖκες ἐξ ἀναστάσεως τοὺς νεκροὺς αὐτῶν· ἄλλοι δὲ ἐτυμπανίσθησαν, οὐ προσδεξάμενοι τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, ἵνα κρείττονος ἀναστάσεως τύχωσιν·
records.gloss: Received women by resurrection the dead of them; others but were tortured, not having accepted the release, so that a better resurrection they might obtain;
pieces: Women had their dead given back to them, raised to life. Others were tortured and beaten, and they would not accept freedom, because they wanted to obtain a better resurrection.

L.35: Women received their dead by resurrection; and others were tortured, not having accepted release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

R.35: Some women had their dead family members raised back to life. Other people were tortured. They refused to give up their faith in order to be set free, because they wanted to be raised to a better life when God raises the dead.

decisions.reason: Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath and gave him back to his mother (1 Kings 17:23), and Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite woman (2 Kings 4:36-37).

2 Maccabees, a Jewish book written in Greek, found in the Greek Old Testament though not in the Hebrew Bible, tells of the elderly Eleazar, who went to the place of torture rather than eat forbidden food (2 Maccabees 6:19, 28), and of seven brothers and their mother, who were tortured to death under King Antiochus IV (about 167 BC). They were offered their freedom if they gave up God's law (7:24), and they died hoping that God would raise them up to everlasting life (7:9, 14, 23).

decisions.choice: were tortured: beaten while stretched on a frame
decisions.reason: τυμπανίζω comes from a word for a drum, and means to torture someone stretched on a frame and beaten. Such torture often ended in death, and the author may mean that they died.

decisions.choice: release: being set free from the torture, on the condition of giving up their faith
decisions.reason: ἀπολύτρωσις usually means redemption or release by payment. Here it is the release the torturers offered, which those tortured would not accept.

decisions.choice: a better resurrection: rising to everlasting life, better than a return to this life
decisions.reason: The women at the start of the verse received their dead back to mortal life; those who were tortured hoped for the resurrection to the life that does not end (6:2; Daniel 12:2).

decisions.choice: refused to give up their faith in order to be set free; when God raises the dead
decisions.reason: Readable says what release would have cost them, following 2 Maccabees 7:24, and what the better resurrection is. The Greek implies these but does not say them.

records.source: ἕτεροι δὲ ἐμπαιγμῶν καὶ μαστίγων πεῖραν ἔλαβον, ἔτι δὲ δεσμῶν καὶ φυλακῆς·
records.gloss: Others and of mockings and of floggings trial received, still and of chains and of prison;
pieces: Others went through mockery and the lash, and beyond that, chains and prison cells.

L.36: And others received [the] trial of mockings and floggings, and still more of chains and prison.

R.36: Others were laughed at and beaten with whips. Some were even put in chains and thrown into prison.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15; 1 Kings 22:24-27; 2 Chronicles 36:16
decisions.reason: Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks and later imprisoned (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15); Micaiah was struck and put in prison (1 Kings 22:24-27); Israel "mocked the messengers of God" (2 Chronicles 36:16). In 2 Maccabees 7:7, 10 the brothers are mocked before they are tortured.

decisions.choice: received trial of: experienced, went through
decisions.reason: πεῖραν ἔλαβον ("to take a trial of") means to experience something; the same phrase is used of the Egyptians in 11:29, who "made trial" of the sea.

records.source: ἐλιθάσθησαν, ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρης ἀπέθανον, περιῆλθον ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν, ὑστερούμενοι, θλιβόμενοι, κακουχούμενοι, ὧν οὐκ ἦν ἄξιος ὁ κόσμος ἐπὶ ἐρημίαις πλανώμενοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς·
records.gloss: They were stoned, they were sawn in two, by murder of sword they died, they went around in sheepskins, in goat skins, being in need, being oppressed, being mistreated, \v 38 of whom not was worthy the world, in deserts wandering and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth.
pieces: They were stoned, sawn in two, cut down by the sword. They roamed about wearing the skins of sheep and goats, lacking everything, oppressed, treated cruelly.
The world did not deserve such people. They wandered over deserts and mountains, and sheltered in caves and in holes in the earth.

L.37: They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they died by murder of [the] sword; they went around in sheepskins, in goat skins, being in need, being oppressed, being mistreated
L.38: (of whom the world was not worthy), wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth.

R.37: Some were killed by having stones thrown at them. Some were cut in two with a saw. Some were killed with swords. Some went from place to place wearing only the skins of sheep and goats. They were poor, they suffered much, and people treated them cruelly.
R.38: The world was not worthy of such people. They wandered in deserts and mountains. They had to hide in caves and in pits dug in the earth.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text: "they were stoned, they were sawn in two"
alternatives: many manuscripts add "they were tempted" (or "tested") before or after "they were sawn in two"
decisions.reason: From general knowledge: a word meaning "they were tempted" stands in many manuscripts, but in different places, and some early witnesses lack it. A word for "tempted" seems out of place among ways of being killed, and it looks very like the words for "sawn" and "burned" in Greek, so it may have come from a copying slip. The SBLGNT leaves it out. Reviewers must check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: 2 Chronicles 24:20-22; 1 Kings 19:10; Jeremiah 26:20-23
decisions.reason: Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22; Matthew 23:35). Being sawn in two is not told in the Old Testament; an old Jewish tradition, found in the Ascension of Isaiah, says that Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh. Prophets were killed with the sword (1 Kings 19:10; Jeremiah 26:23).

μηλωτή is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Elijah's cloak (1 Kings 19:13, 19; 2 Kings 2:13-14); Elijah wore a garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8). Rough skins were the clothing of the poor and of prophets (Zechariah 13:4).

decisions.choice: "of whom the world was not worthy" is a comment set into the description
decisions.reason: The relative clause breaks into the list of participles ("being mistreated ... wandering"). It turns the world's judgment around: those the world drove out were too good for it.

decisions.choice: 1 Kings 18:4, 13; 19:9; 1 Maccabees 2:28-31; 2 Maccabees 6:11
decisions.reason: Obadiah hid a hundred prophets in caves (1 Kings 18:4, 13), Elijah lodged in a cave (1 Kings 19:9), and in the Maccabean persecution faithful Jews fled to the mountains and hid in caves (1 Maccabees 2:28-31; 2 Maccabees 6:11).

decisions.choice: mistreated: the same kind of suffering Moses chose to share (11:25)
decisions.reason: κακουχέομαι is the simple form of the verb used in 11:25 (συγκακουχέομαι, "to be mistreated together with"); it appears again in 13:3.

decisions.choice: killed by having stones thrown at them; cut in two with a saw; killed with swords
alternatives: stoned; sawn in two; died by the sword
decisions.reason: Readable explains each form of death in plain words and adds "some", since not all suffered every one.

records.source: καὶ πάντες μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν, τοῦ θεοῦ περὶ ἡμῶν κρεῖττόν τι προβλεψαμένου, ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσιν.
records.gloss: And these all having been attested through the faith not received the promise, \v 40 the God for us something better having foreseen, so that not apart from us they would be made perfect.
pieces: Through their faith all of these were attested by God, and yet they did not receive the promise.
God had in view something better for us: they were not to be made perfect apart from us.

L.39: And all these, having been attested through faith, did not receive the promise,
L.40: God having foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us.

R.39: God approved of all these people because of their faith. But none of them received what God had promised.
R.40: God had planned something better that would include us. They will not be made complete without us. We will reach the goal together.

decisions.choice: all these were attested: God's witness, as in 11:2
decisions.reason: The chapter ends as it began (11:2) with the verb "attested": God's witness to their faith, recorded in Scripture.

decisions.choice: the promise: the final inheritance God promised, not yet given
decisions.reason: They received particular promises (11:33), but not "the promise": the eternal inheritance (9:15), the heavenly city (11:10, 16), the rest God promised (4:1). This is the promise the readers must endure to receive (10:36).

decisions.choice: foreseen, provided: God planned in advance
decisions.reason: προβλέπομαι means to see beforehand and so to plan or provide. God's plan included something better that would come with the new covenant (7:19, 22; 8:6).

decisions.choice: made perfect: brought to the goal, the full salvation of the new covenant, together with Christ's people
decisions.reason: As at 2:10, to be "made perfect" means to be brought to the goal. Christ "has perfected for all time those who are being made holy" by his one offering (10:14), and in 12:23 the author speaks of "the spirits of the righteous made perfect". The faithful of old reach that goal only with those who believe in Christ, through what he has done.

decisions.choice: made complete; reach the goal
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "made perfect". Readable says "made complete", as the book allows, because "perfect" in everyday English suggests being without fault rather than being brought to the goal.

decisions.choice: attested by God; God approved of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the one who bore witness (see 11:2).
